Our team successfully developed and implemented photonic solutions for several signal processing tasks relevant to astrophotonic spectrometers, utilizing integrated photonics technology. This involves implementing spectral cross-correlation (SCC), a technique employed in exoplanet detection with traditional spectrometers. Our research showcases the feasibility of this approach by comparing photonic and electronic implementations of SCC, achieving high consistency between them. The integration of SCC with SCC-based exoplanet detection algorithms further highlights its potential. Notably, our photonic solution offers significant advantages, including compactness, reliability, and cost savings. The use of on-chip spectrometers enabled by integrated photonics may allow a substantial reduction in cost and form factor, potentially paving the way for more efficient and cost-effective exoplanet detection systems.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, enhancing drug repurposing, and identifying new drug indications. This paper reviews and categorizes these advanced models into four main concepts: mapping drugs to feature spaces, building complex drug relationships, matching drug pairs, and predicting multiple labels. Furthermore, it proposes a framework to guide the selection of models based on the specific, practical constraints associated with real-world applications.

Identifying damaged roads is a challenging task, and current deep learning methods struggle when applied to new countries due to the need for extensive recalibration. This problem can be addressed by using transfer learning, which allows a model trained in one place to be effectively used in another. Our approach leverages pre-trained transfer learning to create a robust, general-purpose system for road damage detection across various contexts. We evaluate and compare three transfer learning strategies on a comprehensive dataset consisting of road images from seven different countries. The results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly when using features pre-trained on large-scale image datasets. This leads to improved accuracy in road damage detection and easier deployment of road inspection models in new countries without the need for retraining.

Imitation learning enables robots to acquire tasks by watching humans perform them in other domains, but directly observing humans in the same environment is often impractical. Therefore, robots can train on existing video datasets and apply their learned skills to real-world tasks. Current approaches rely on paired data from both human and target domains, which is seldom available. This research presents a novel framework that enables cross-domain imitation learning with only unpaired data. This approach enables the robot to identify and adapt to domain-specific characteristics and extract common actions across different environments. To evaluate the framework, we conducted a suite of manipulation tasks using two distinct robotic systems.

A major unresolved issue in high-redshift galaxy formation is the link between the first stars and galaxies. One hypothesis suggests that the first stars formed within mini-galaxies, triggering rapid collapse and the emergence of fragmentation. However, simulations of this process often result in multiple star clusters, which may hinder the mini-galaxy's ability to form a single dominant black hole. This could lead to fewer large black holes at early galaxy stages, affecting the link between high-redshift galaxies and black holes. Our team analyzed the relationship between the first stars and galaxies by modeling a Population III star and a mini-galaxy in a 3D simulation. Our results show that strong magnetic fields can prevent galaxy fragmentation, allowing the star cluster to consolidate into a single black hole, increasing the link between high-redshift galaxies and black holes.

Association rules have become a staple in data mining, particularly for uncovering hidden patterns in categorical data. Deduction, the process of inferring new rules from an existing set, is a natural consequence of this approach, a common finding in numerous studies. This document explores the concept of redundancy in association rules, defining a redundant rule as one that can be deduced from the rest of the set given. A new class of deduction schemes is introduced, each offering a distinct notion of redundancy. This framework generalizes previous findings and provides a specific focus on the largest and smallest bases for the particular reduction scheme associated with closed itemsets. By establishing the criteria for redundancy and presenting a relevant closure operation, we prove that any particular reduction scheme associated with itemsets can be carried out using this operation.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health issues. For a long time, the rehabilitation process involved assigning them to substance abuse and mental health treatment, but there has been little evidence supporting the effectiveness of this approach. A recent study seeks to fill this knowledge gap by examining the impact of a policy in Massachusetts, which made cognitive-behavioral therapy compulsory for individuals convicted of nonviolent crimes who were sent to the state's prison hospital. By comparing those affected and those not affected by the policy, along with examining various hospital outcomes, the study finds that this policy led to reduced recidivism and hospital readmission rates, but increased new charges that were more violent in nature.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach for creating heterogeneous wireless networks that are smart and self-configuring. They can also be used in adaptive, context-aware applications like wireless charging, fast network convergence, and beamforming techniques. However, gathering the necessary data for radio maps is a challenging task that requires significant manpower and time. To simplify this process, we propose a new method where unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) collect spectrum information at various locations, and a central control system uses this data to create radio maps. This innovative method requires the vehicles to transmit real-time data, and the control system to consolidate this information, leading to more up-to-date and accurate maps. A key feature of our method is that it compensates for data synchronization issues that arise due to transmission delays and creates the radio maps in real-time. This innovative method enables the creation of high-quality radio maps while saving significant amounts of time and resources.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time-series data representing continuous processes. By leveraging Hidden Markov Models to model system behaviors, GLA detects anomalies that deviate significantly from normal system operations. GLA's effectiveness is demonstrated through an examination of real-world log sequences from the Kepler space telescope, produced by a faulty system component. Furthermore, GLA's suitability is explored in the context of power plant operations, process monitoring, and real-time control applications.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification using sound, visual, and thermal imagery. By combining this multimodal technique with traditional 2D image analysis, our studies on synthetic and real datasets show that sound and visual imagery can individually contribute unique information, while using both in a verification system yields improved overall performance. Furthermore, our experiments using thermal data on a separate person identification task also demonstrate its potential to augment sound, visual, and thermal imagery.

Generating new training examples by manipulating existing data is known as data augmentation, with applications in multiple fields. However, significantly modified approaches were typically required for significant gains in NLP and neural machine translation, whereas significant improvements were observed in computer vision using simpler methods. Inspired by these findings, we investigate the impact of similar data augmentation techniques on automatic speech recognition and discover that simpler methods yield significant improvements without major modifications to the recognition framework. We present a unified framework for implementing these techniques in automatic speech recognition and translation. Our experiments utilizing this unified framework were conducted on the AMI meeting corpus and librispeech dataset, yielding notable improvements in word error rate.

When estimating the mean of distribution mixtures with overlapping distributions, traditional estimation methods often struggle due to the difficulty of modeling the entire distribution. To overcome this challenge, we propose estimating the mean of the mixture directly without needing to model its full distribution. To do this, we develop an algorithm for computing the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of the mean of the mixture, as well as other parameters involved. However, finding the maximum likelihood estimate (MLi) of each individual component is an NP-hard problem. Therefore, we create a generalized iterative maximization method to efficiently compute a local ML estimate for the mixture parameters. The proposed method involves solving simpler subproblems and shows that the generated solution sequence converges to a local ML estimate. Applications of this method are explored in two scenarios: continuous sampling and discrete sampling. The method's performance is demonstrated using simulated data and real-data examples.

Achieving comprehensive privacy protection for all attributes simultaneously is an insurmountable task. Thus, our approach focuses on safeguarding specific target attributes, allowing non-target attributes to be disclosed indirectly. This constitutes a novel problem, known as one-sided differential privacy, and we devise two strategies to implement it while minimizing privacy compromises for the involved attributes. One strategy allocates uniform privacy budgets to all attributes, resulting in at least one non-target attribute being misreported with an unpredictable value. The other strategy misreports target attributes with randomly generated values, leading to potential leakage of information about their utility. In contrast, our first protocol distributes variable privacy budgets, allowing us to quantify and limit the misreporting probabilities of target attributes. Consequently, we can also restrict the loss utility and effectively limit potential leakage information. Our methods were put to the test in a real-world scenario involving noisy location data release, and we observed substantial improvements over existing approaches.

In protoplanetary disks, the effect of gas and dust on molecular line emission is significant.
We utilized Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales (MAPS) to analyze a specific disk around a young star called LkCa15.
This study involved [CII] and CO observations, which revealed a central cavity and an inner edge.
Compared to other young stars, the LkCa15 disk shows complex [CII] emission patterns.
We found that [CII] emission in LkCa15 does not vary with dust emission as seen in other young stars.
We analyzed two possible explanations for this phenomenon: (1) gas and dust separation and (2) gas processing through chemical mechanisms.
We found that (1) the dust surface density in LkCa15 does not match its gas surface density.
(2) The LkCa15 disk's [CII]/CO ratio is significantly higher than expected.
We concluded that gas processing through chemical mechanisms is the primary cause of [CII] emission in this young star.
Further observations are necessary to determine the origin of [CII] emission in young stars and disprove the role of gas and dust separation.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've developed the 'timeb', a Python-based toolkit that facilitates the analysis of time-stamped measurements, enabling the efficient extraction of valuable insights. This tool incorporates a range of features including data collection, visualization, filtering, clustering, and correlation calculations, all backed by a flexible, scriptable, and customizable design. Its architecture is both versatile and adaptable, allowing the integration of new methods and techniques while maintaining consistency with the established toolbox methods.

We prove the existence of mild solutions for a mean field game where the dynamics are constrained within a closed domain and the state cannot exit this domain infinitely quickly. The analysis relies on techniques that combine Hilbertian and $L^1$ arguments, making the existence result applicable in more general settings beyond those typically handled.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted a thorough examination of these structures, which were previously identified by analyzing deviations in Gaia's astrometric parallax measurements, and by investigating their properties and composition. Additionally, we explored the connection between these structures and ridges detected in the Gaia sky color distribution to verify a previously proposed hypothesis. By combining Gaia data with photometric information from the APASS survey, we further investigated the stellar population of these structures, addressing potential biases. Our analysis shows that most stellar strings have a projection across the galactic plane and consist primarily of stars with ages around 1 billion years. Some structures exhibit parallax anomalies due to nearby high-luminosity stars, and we found evidence for extragalactic stars in Gaia data associated with these structures. We found a connection between stellar strings and Gaia sky color distribution ridges, contradicting the theory of a common origin, and instead supporting the theory that both are influenced by the Milky Way's main stellar population. Our findings also disprove the claim that stellar strings originate from the main galactic plane populations identified by cross-match data, and we found significant evidence for young stellar populations within some structures.

For visual apparel retailers, identifying visually incompatible outfits is a crucial task.
To address this, we introduce a novel dataset, VICTOR, consisting of outfit
images, complete with outfit visual incompatibility labels, to support outfit
visual learning. To achieve effective contrastive learning, we pre-train a
visual backbone on the proposed dataset, combining fashion-aware contrastive
pre-training with self-supervised training. Additionally, our proposed outfit
visual incompatibility detection method, based on contrastive learning,
resulted in improved performance on multiple outfit visual incompatibility
benchmarks. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance on several
related outfit visual tasks.

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, offering a systematic approach to defining and quantifying quantum effects such as entanglement, nonlocality, and nonclassicality. This approach allows for targeted applications of specific quantum properties. In the context of optical systems, recent developments have expanded the resource theory of nonclassical light to include broader scenarios, encompassing both single-time measurements and spectral distributions. This article provides a comprehensive overview of these latest breakthroughs, focusing on the formalization of optical resource theory and its practical implications.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research involving the Swampland program has led to a prediction of a compact dimension with a radius no larger than the Planck length. Another prediction suggests that the Planck mass is not an upper limit, but rather that it is about 10 times the mass of an intermediate black hole. These predictions imply that dark matter should comprise nearly all of the universe within this extra dimension. Given the new constraints from primordial black holes, these findings suggest that the fraction of dark matter made up of primordial black holes should be around 10^-3 or greater.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model to study materials' fracture, particularly when rare events of breaking apart dominate. Using the driving force as a parameter, we observe how introducing bonds with finite strength and energy affects the transition from small to large rifts. In the existing model, without bonds, the system experiences only small rifts up to a certain threshold, after which a major rupture forms. With a finite number of bonds, we see an intermediate stage where many smaller rifts form as the threshold is approached, and the analysis of their sizes follows universal principles, influenced by how many bonds are broken. Furthermore, we find that the rift that forms near the threshold has characteristics similar to those in entirely broken systems, and this forms a distinct category with its own properties. Using these features, we create a simplified model that replicates the dynamic process of forming rifts, capturing both how they vary over time and space, and we compare this to another model that describes a system with no bonds.

The main challenge hindering the development of efficient GaN transistors lies in its moiré structure when attempting to find a suitable lattice-matched substrate. In this study, two materials - ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ - were discovered to be compatible substrates for GaN, offering a solution to this problem. By incorporating intentional strain into GaN layers, researchers found that the material's hole mobility is significantly enhanced in a specific direction, thus maximizing its performance. This innovative approach to GaN's substrate matching paves the way for improved GaN transistor technology.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes a key limitation in traditional policy gradient methods, which rely on a vast amount of training data to navigate robotic systems in complex, real-world environments. Our innovative method employs an extremely compact neural network, trained using extremely compressed pixel data from sensors, which overcomes extremely high exploration costs associated with traditional methods. Traditional policy gradient methods use full data and a full temporal difference loss, which often forces a trade-off in exploring the environment. Our new method, based on the sparse regression framework, uses time-aliased data and performs subsampling, resulting in a more efficient learning process. We demonstrate this new approach using a model-free strategy in the complex task of navigating through dense forest environments with only visual information, which we accomplish using Enduro, a small autonomous underwater vehicle. Our experiment shows that we can successfully navigate around large rocks and through narrow passages, while collecting a significantly smaller amount of data compared to traditional methods.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a quadratic differential with a singularities restriction. The limitations on these singularities allow the use of holomorphic 1-forms to express the normal component of the geodesic curvature, which in turn enables the definition of isothermic properties. The surface is constructed based on a frame and its associated connections, and it can be shown that it possesses isothermic properties with a conformal metric and an isothermic second fundamental form. However, in instances where the quadratic differential's order is increased, both the metric and the quadratic form increase in order accordingly. The Gauduchon metric remains invariant under the Calapso transformation but not the Hopf transformation. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the Gauduchon metric, the Hopf and Calapso transformations, and the extended Hopf formula.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $Ef(x) = E(f(X)|X(x))$, with special emphasis on its application to solving the Fokker-Planck equation via zero-finding methods. To evaluate approximation errors for this problem, with respect to both source smoothness and the influence of stochastic noise, we conduct a comprehensive study in a nonparametric setting. By imposing different noise conditions, including sub-Gaussian, polynomial, and no noise scenarios, we determine optimal rates of convergence. To facilitate this, we introduce the concept of approximating conditional expectations using approximating measures, with its associated approximating operators.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim et al. and Kim--Zhang by examining $\lambda$-analogues of well-known Stirling numbers of the second kind with restricted run lengths, as well as $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind with the same constraint. It investigates their overlapping properties and generates analogous identities.

Temporally-tagged Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) have become essential in representing dynamic real-world information. By tagging the knowledge graph with temporal labels, trends can be identified, which in turn enables the inference of unobserved facts. Previous approaches to tackling link prediction in TKGs have relied on modeling the evolution of relationships, but this paper proposes a different approach by using a comprehensive static model that captures various temporal patterns, rather than predicting time stamps. By using this static model, reasoning capabilities are enhanced, which in turn improves overall performance. When combined with an attention-based entity representation, the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in multiple benchmarks, demonstrating its efficacy in tackling link prediction tasks.

This note demonstrates that a finite graph equivalence inherently implies strong shift equivalence. This relationship enables us to derive a criterion for finite graph strong shift equivalence based on algebraic isomorphisms of associated C*-algebras and line bundle isomorphisms. Consequently, we establish that two row-finite graphs are strongly shift equivalent if and only if their associated C*-algebras are matrix-algebra twisted isomorphic.

In this research, we have examined the complex tomographic structure of gluon exchanges that influence quarkonium dissociation in a strong magnetic field, considering all possible gluon propagator interactions. The tomographic approach allows us to analyze how the gluon exchange influences quarkonium binding in different spatial directions, providing insights into the anisotropic quarkonium dissociation. The study focuses on the anomalous gluon propagator effects and how they interact with quarkonium in the presence of a strong magnetic field. The tomographic analysis reveals that quarkonium dissociation is indeed an anisotropic process and that direction-specific form factors can provide insights into this phenomenon. The study utilizes the worldline formalism and perturbation theory to compute the tomographic influence of heavy quark pairs on quarkonium dissociation in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. However, not every query can be answered solely through a knowledge graph, so the model needs to supply missing information, but this process is inefficient to scale up. Our solution includes a specialized module that can handle complex queries by integrating graph reasoning with language modeling, allowing for an answer to be given with minimal knowledge base lookups. We test this approach on two challenging datasets and achieve top results, outperforming other models by 3 points on the dataset where knowledge base queries are most scarce, while also providing a detailed analysis of the process and performance.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a crucial role in theoretical computer science and have been successfully applied in various areas. Our method generalizes the concept of covers to higher dimensions, offering both a theoretical framework and practical applications. The constructed high dimensional expanders can be used to create efficient codes and provide new insights into spectral properties.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Betti and de Rham realizations of the $\mathscr L$-invariant associated with Artin motives. This generalizes previously calculated $p$-adic $L$-functions for general Artin motives, as well as specific cases such as Hecke cusp forms and Dirichlet characters. Furthermore, by examining the growth of these invariants within Iwasawa theory, some $p$-adic analogues of central theorem can be derived.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electromagnetic fields is a difficult but crucial task with significant implications. This current research introduces a novel Rydberg multifrequency MW detection method. Using aluminum-doped lithium yttrbium oxide, which exhibits strong nonlinearity when influenced by resonant near-field enhancement, our detection system leverages deep learning to accurately identify and distinguish between various frequency bands. This can lead to novel applications in astronomical research and the observation of cosmic phenomena.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally massive spiral galaxy, exhibits remarkable characteristics despite its distance. Utilizing high-resolution data from Keck/MOSFIRE, this study examines the galaxy's properties. The analysis reveals that UGC 8839 has a relatively small half-light diameter of 2.64 kpc. Additionally, kinematic modeling indicates a exceptionally high dynamic mass within its half-light radius, amounting to 1011.44 solar masses. This is coupled with a low rotation curve flattening value of 0.21, suggesting significant mass. However, the derived dynamical mass is 12 times greater than the stellar mass, whereas the minimum galactic mass required to prevent the dispersal of its gas is only 3 times the minimum required to retain its bulge. This unusual situation might be attributed to the recent onset of significant star formation in UGC 8839, occurring about 100 million years ago, during which its gas and star formation rates peaked. The unusually high dynamical mass could also be a result of an unusually large average stellar mass in the galaxy, a characteristic often observed in massive, compact, and rich galaxies, although the lack of a detected metal line precludes this explanation.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set.

Using thresholding techniques, gravity wave signatures in the ionosphere of Mars are detected and analyzed for their characteristics such as wavelength, propagation, and oscillation periods. These waves are identified through continuous changes in ionospheric height and electron density, detected by MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN ionospheric profilers. The study's findings are compared with previous work on gravity waves in the thermosphere, revealing similarities in wave behavior. Wave activity patterns are analyzed in relation to the local time and season in which the waves were detected. The results indicate that gravity waves detected by MGS, ODY, MRO, and MAVEN exhibit varying wave lengths and propagation patterns. Notably, seasons affecting the waves detected by MGS, ODY, and MAVEN suggest preferences for specific wave types and directions. In contrast, the waves detected by MRO show no such seasonal trends.

The ALICE experiment at LHC has been studying various aspects of Ultra-Peripheral Collisions (UPCs) in Pb-Pb at a $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 5.02$ TeV energy. UCPs in heavy ion collisions offer a unique opportunity to examine VMD, photon gloun fusion, and forward J/psi production in lead-on-lead collisions. A recently published study using LHCb and ATLAS data, in collaboration with simulations from PHENIX, presents new insights into forward J/psi production in UPCs at high energies. Measuring the production cross-sections of J/psi in both photon-lead and photon-proton collisions provides essential information about nucleon structure, particularly the generalized parton distribution (GPDH) at extremely low x values. Ultimately, these studies contribute to furthering our understanding of proton structure, particularly at the boundary between photon and hadronic interactions.

Recently, end-to-end visually guided sound generation models, such as AudioFormer, have been proposed to learn realistic sound generation from direct audio-video pairs. However, existing audio-transformer based methods struggle with realistic sound synthesis, particularly in producing the desired sound duration and pitch. In this research, we introduce SoundDurationControl, a modular module integrated with AudioFormer to enable precise control over sound duration and duration-conditioned sound generation. Its core component is a flow-based time-transformer network, learning an implicit mapping between latent sound sequences and latent video features. Building upon this foundation, we demonstrate that AudioFormer coupled with SoundDurationControl outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in sound generation tasks, including sound transformation and sound insertion. Furthermore, we open-source our model and data at https://github.com/FeiyangFeng/LongDurationSoundGeneration.

Recurrent Neural Networks have emerged as a leading framework for processing sequential data, yet their effectiveness is not entirely clear. This paper provides theoretical insights into their performance by comparing it to a basic recurrent model that only captures the previous output. We show that Recurrent Neural Networks can efficiently learn and represent temporal information, but only if they are designed to capture the state of the system at each time step. Our analysis also confirms the universality of Recurrent Neural Networks, making them suitable for a wide range of tasks, and highlights their advantage in capturing long-term dependencies. In particular, we discovered that architectures like Long Short-Term Memory networks can effectively learn to represent and utilize temporal information, whereas Simple Recurrent Models are limited in their capacity to capture more than one step of temporal dependence.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate countermeasures, aligned with economic projections, impacts the pandemic's progression over extended periods. The study reveals that a timely and consistently applied 'transient' policy can provide benefits similar to those of an 'optimal' policy, underscoring the importance of the timing and consistency of measures rather than the specific magnitude of restrictions. This finding holds across a wide range of economic scenarios, making it universally applicable. The study emphasizes the value of adherence to pandemic control guidelines for maximizing both health benefits and economic gains.

The objective of data debugging is to pinpoint inaccuracies and biases within training datasets, posing a complex challenge due to the numerous potential issues that can arise and the variety of possible impacts each one can have. In this research, Shapley values are employed to import key data points that influence machine learning model training. By training individual sub-pipelines, each focused on a particular aspect of model performance, the authors can effectively balance the detection of various types of errors, including bias and inaccuracy. This approach is tested on three diverse datasets, each requiring different evaluations, and on a custom image classification task with an imposed dataset constraint.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study establishes pressure as a reliable method for controlling the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn single crystals, exhibiting significant Hall resistance that outperforms composition-based approaches. The pressure required to achieve this effect is pressure-controlled without needing exact chemical substitution. Pressure gradually transforms the triangular antiferromagnetism in Mn$_3$Sn into hexagonal structures, ultimately returning to MnSn. A pressure-controlled phase transition can reversibly toggle the anomalous Hall effect, exhibiting a change in sign and varying magnitude. Our findings highlight pressure as a new approach to managing the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn.

Formal knowledge representation, particularly in the form of logic-based knowledge graphs, has long been preferred in AI but is hindered by a lack of suitable training data. A key challenge lies in identifying relational connections between entities described in natural language, a task known as relation extraction. Enabled by recent advancements in deep neural networks, this task can now be efficiently accomplished, allowing for the construction of knowledge graphs from extensive text data using learning-based methods. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of deep learning methods for relation extraction and an associated large-scale dataset, thereby facilitating the formulation and efficient solution of this essential knowledge engineering problem.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a large, unknown domain $\Omega$ and a small ball of radius $\delta$ centered at point $p$. We then analyze the following Steklov-Robin problem: finding $u$ and $\lambda$ such that the negative Laplacian of $u$ equals $\lambda u$ within the domain, with the condition that the sum of the negative gradient of $u$ and $\beta\delta^\alpha$ times $u$ at point $p$ equals zero. Here, $\beta$ and $\alpha$ are given constants, and we assume $\alpha > 0$. 

Our main contribution lies in investigating the first Steklov-Robin eigenfunction and eigenvalue for this particular class of domains. In doing so, we introduce a new class of approximating Laplacian operators that incorporate boundary contributions and are consistent with the given Steklov-Robin problem in the given homogenization limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate the convergence of Eigenvalues as $\delta$ approaches zero, and establish explicit formulas for Eigenvalues in specific cases, such as when $\alpha=1$.

We investigate a hypergraph reconstruction problem where the goal is to derive a hypergraph from a given matrix that represents its signed and weighted node connections. To address this, we propose a novel hyperedge detection method based on a combinatorial objective function. Due to the inherent difficulty of this objective, we develop a new algorithm, i.e., the Supergraph Reconstruction Network, a deep neural model that efficiently captures and exploits the underlying structure of hyperedges. Through rigorous analysis and extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach i Supergraph Detection on benchmark datasets is robust and outperforms state-ofthe-art methods in various graph-to-hypergraph transformations.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document their visual analysis of imaging techniques and diagnostic findings.  Precise identification of abnormalities like tumors or fractures is crucial for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.  Traditional radiology report annotation methods are time-consuming and yield poor results due to the abstract nature of text and two-dimensional image representation.  Our solution involves aligning radiology report text with pixel-level image data using minimal manual annotation through CT projection of radiographic landmarks.  This innovation enables the integration of radiologists' visual diagnosis with computer vision and machine learning techniques, thus unlocking new possibilities for radiological modernization.  Our approach is supported by substantial manual annotation efforts across 1000 pairs of chest X-rays and CT scans, along with automatic annotation for the remaining 27,000 pairs.

Bill Thurston initially found that any tight contact structure on a surface-tore boundary 3-manifold has an Euler class that satisfies $e_D(\xi) \geq 0$. In contrast, a recent finding by Le Roux showed a tight contact structure exists where $e_D(\xi)$ can be strictly less than or equal to $0$. In this research, specific conditions for $e_D(\xi)$ to be positive, negative, or zero are set. By utilizing these criteria, $e_D(\xi)$ values for tight contact structures on certain manifolds like integer-surgery on the positive twist of the knot $8_{19}$ and the manifold $dL$ are determined, where $L$ is the figure-eight knot, and a contact structure on $dL$ is constructed, where $e_D(\xi)=0$, which has a particular characteristicistric surface $P$, whose norm is minimum.

In this investigation, we explore the concept of directional emission in 
microcavity lasers through the lens of entropy production rate, proportionate to 
the product of specific probability distributions for intensity and momentum 
in the free space above the device. We demonstrate that this entropy production 
rate serves as a reliable metric for quantifying the directionality of emission 
across an array of microcavity lasers operating in single and multi-mode 
configurations. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying pump positions on 
the overall entropy production rate in these configurations.

Our investigation assesses the price stability of various cryptocurrencies as a means of transaction across different time periods and evaluates their effectiveness compared to major traditional currencies. We utilize the prices of cryptocurrencies in multiple local currencies to analyze their price stability, allowing us to compare their performance against established traditional currencies. The results of this analysis reveal significant variations in the price stability of cryptocurrencies, with some currencies like Litecoin, Litecoin Cash, Decred and Cardano showing price stability comparable to major traditional currencies like the euro, US dollar and British pound. Furthermore, our data suggests that certain cryptocurrencies have experienced an improvement in price stability in recent years. When considering the probability of price changes exceeding certain thresholds, we find that some cryptocurrencies are less reliable than traditional currencies, with the difference being most pronounced in the short term. However, in the long term, this reliability gap narrows significantly, suggesting that prices of these currencies may converge over extended periods of time.

By integrating analytical methods from the inverse scattering of the Zakharov-Shabat system, we have derived novel finite noise exponent relations for the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. This approach surpasses previous finite noise exponent schemes and converges to the exact infinite noise exponent results.

The solar wind's compressive turbulence at sub-ion scales is examined. We analyze magnetic and density fluctuations from the MMS mission within a compressive turbulent range. This study uses a comprehensive approach, starting at large scales and progressing through various scales, ultimately reaching the expected sub-ion cutoff. We calculate key spectral measures, including energy and cascade rates, and compare our results to theoretical predictions. Our research demonstrates that both Alfv\'en and Kelvin-Helmholtz waves exhibit similar behavior, with inverse-cascade-like phenomena occurring at mesoscales and $-5/3$ slope characteristics appearing at smaller scales. Notably, these observations hold true for both kinetic and compressive components.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are often constrained by the coherence time, especially at higher wavelengths in soft X-rays. This can pose a challenge for studying atomic processes. Our research shows that modifying the chirp-taper technique allows for overcoming this limitation, making it possible to generate attosecond pulses even deep within the soft X-ray range. Our simulations indicate that by applying a negative magnetic field during the taper region with a carefully chosen frequency, the electron bunch can maintain its short pulse duration, even when using longer electron beams and magnetically chirped beams. This solution brings pulse durations close to the atomic limit, facilitating direct observation of various atomic processes.

A numerical proof is provided for the asymptotic approximation of linearly stratified flows with viscosity, using physical optics approximations as the Brunt-V\"{a}is\"{a}l\'{a} frequency and molecular viscosity tend toward zero. This is achieved by applying the geometric optics approximation to the acoustic pressure in shear waves within the method of multiple scales. It is observed that the amplitude equations governing the shear wave consist of two coupled heat and wave equations.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in several real-world experiments utilizing Texas population
data, where it has demonstrated the ability to reject highly gerrymastered plans
while accepting fairer ones.

This research introduces a novel defect detection method specifically designed for patterned fabric images, addressing the limitations of existing methods, including difficulties in detecting defects and distinguishing patterns. The proposed method, based on GHOG, GHOG, and matrix low-rank decomposition, begins by generating a gradient direction histogram oriented in a specific direction, followed by a template creation process, and finally, a low-rank decomposition of a generated tensor. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on artificially defective fabric images.

To enhance the robustness of agents in reinforcement learning, especially those navigating complex environments, we introduce a new regularization method inspired by information theory. This method encourages agents to gather sufficient data during exploration to maximize policy uncertainty, thus expanding their navigation capabilities. Our experiments, conducted in visually-based navigation tasks within synthetic environments, demonstrate that this regularization method significantly enhances policy uncertainty diversification, resulting in improved generalization and more efficient exploration compared to standard approaches.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at infinity, our research demonstrates that the Bondi mass cannot decrease faster than a specific rate. This rate is determined by the space of conformal Killing vectors at that infinity. Assuming that the fundamental particles emitting radiation have spins greater than or equal to 1, our research provides a general spacetime constraint that applies to all such spacetimes, rather than being limited to specific gravitational wave metrics. This constraint can be seen as a macroscopic form of mass dimension analysis, potentially applicable across spacetime theories.

We examine the formation of Population III binary black holes (BBBs) within nuclear star clusters using a combination of simulations. The probability of these BBBs forming and merging within a specific cluster depends on several factors, including the initial metallic content, stellar mass allocation, spatial distribution of stars, cluster mass, and the environment in which the cluster is hosted. Below the metallicity of $10^{-2}$ times that of the sun, most BBBs form through direct collapse of a binary star system, while higher metallicity allows for the formation of Population II BBBs. The characteristics of BBBs that form within nuclear star clusters vary depending on metallicity, with less massive BBBs found in systems with lower metallicity, and BBBs with mass ratios closer to one. Our analysis reveals that BBBs that form within nuclear star clusters tend to have higher spins, especially those with lower mass ratios, which is consistent with BBBs that would merge as gravitational waves. Below the metallicity of $10^{-1}$ times that of the sun, our findings are consistent with BBBs that would merge as gravitational waves detected by LIGO, while nuclear star clusters with higher metallicity may be the origin of some BBBs detected by LIGO up to redshift 5. Our analysis also allows for estimation of the contribution of nuclear star clusters to the gravitational waves signal from BBBs, which is highly sensitive to factors including the initial metallic content, mass function, and cluster properties.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate domain knowledge or parameter settings. It encompasses the development of multivariate time series detection methods, feature extraction, and the adaptation of existing unsupervised techniques to handle time series information. The proposed method is validated through computer-generated data and real-world data containing information about actual ESS malfunctions.

Our study delves into key decay aspects of the $X(3872)$, an enigmatic X-boson, with a focus on its $J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $J/\psi \pi\pi \pi \gamma$ decay modes, utilizing isospin analysis. The $X(3872)$'s isospin violation during $J/\psi \pi \gamma$ decay is primarily attributed to its mass Compton effect, with a calculated coefficient of $O(100)$, given its $12$ MeV mass gap between the $D^0 \bar{D}^{*0}$ and $D^+ \bar{D}^{-}$, $D^s \bar{D}^{*0}$ thresholds, with the $O(10)$ isospin breaking parameter. The breaking of isospin in $X(3872)$'s $J/\psi \pi\pi \gamma$ decay is controlled by its electric $O(10)$ magnetic transition, with magnetic transition dominating over the $O(100)$ mass Compton effect. The $X(3872)$'s decay into $\psi \pi \gamma$ is dominated by its $O(100)$ mass Compton effect, with decay into $\psi \pi^+ \pi^- \gamma$ and $\psi \pi^0 \

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge, but previous simulations ran significantly slower than other AI tests. Our new proposal, TextWorld Express, offers a faster version of these games, enabling up to one million simulations per second and fostering studies at previously unexplored scales. We also present Textworld Express Huge, a massive platform supporting millions of games, allowing for large-scale investigations.

Using geometric theory, we establish a rigorous framework that extends modelled tensor fields to spaces featuring singularities and carefully analyzes its implications for Topological Insulators possessing defects. The proposed connection between homotopy classes and the effective Brillouin zone, initially demonstrated for defect-free systems, is now generalized to defective Topological Insulators by introducing a new geometric model based on a fiber bundle with a singular base and a locally constant section. Our method resolves a previously unaddressed problem concerning the well-definedness of homotopy classes in spaces with singularities and enables the successful application of geometric tools, such as index theories, to Topological Insulators possessing defects.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $\nu$ ranges from 1 to infinity, and $\Sigma$ consists of two rays originating from the origin at an angle of $2\nu$ radians, with $\Sigma_0$ denoting $\Sigma$ excluding the origin. Now, $\mathcal{A}$ is a class of positive functions, which, when extended to $\Sigma$, are P-harmonic in $\Sigma$ and log-harmonic near the origin. It turns out that such functions, $u$, can be represented as $u(x) = u(r,\theta) = r^{\mu(\theta)}u_0(r)$, with log-harmonic $u_0$ and $\mu$ a multiplicity function, and we provide an estimate for $|\mu|$.

Using a joint multivariate extension of the PEW model, the paper by Katz et al.
provides a framework for analyzing extreme events, which is applied to investigate
the most severe ocean environments in Australia. Specifically, the model is used
to examine the worst storms impacting Port Hedland and Hamilton Island over the
period of 1975-2015, focusing on two variables: 10-meter wind speed and direction.
After identifying parameters for individual sites, the parameters for relative
wind are derived. Employing the parameters, the paper presents return level curves
for various return periods, visualizing dangerous zones and analyzing environmental
factors that influence extreme storms at the two locations.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept in robotic manipulation, called manipulability domain, helps robots safely and efficiently perform various tasks. Most advanced manipulation techniques are tested on advanced research robots with precise movement capabilities. However, to transfer this data to real-world robots, their manipulability space must be adapted due to differences in their kinematics. Traditional methods use probability distribution matching, but these can be computationally expensive. In contrast, we propose a simple transformation method that aligns the manipulability spaces of different robots. This is achieved by transporting data measured on a precise research robot to a real-world robot, making transfer learning possible. The transformation is determined using an iterative iteratively closest point algorithm that accounts for the complex structure of this space. Results show that this method successfully adapts the manipulability space, allowing transfer learning to improve performance.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, we focus on proton-proton collisions with an invariant Higgs boson pair mass range of 115-150 GeV and centre-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ and 14 TeV. By incorporating the full final state kinematics into the calculation of matrix elements and incorporating experimental data, we demonstrate that sufficiently accurate top-quark pair subtraction can be achieved even at lower centre-of-mass energies. However, higher energy experiments at 14 TeV show improved performance due to an increased Higgs boson pair to top quark pair ratio.

A novel method is introduced for training object3D pose estimation models, leveraging accidentally created images of rotating objects in a controlled environment. Since these images are formed without deliberate intervention, the approach simplifies data creation and enhances accuracy by learning from naturally occurring perspectives. Additionally, it overcomes limitations of existing datasets that are restricted to objects with front-facing views, allowing for complete 3D pose recovery. A new type of marking system is proposed to optimize results, and a fundamental geometric analysis of the problem is possible due to the inherent structure of the accidentally created data. Finally, the method's effectiveness is verified through comprehensive benchmarking.

Despite significant attention being paid to COVID-19 vaccine misinformation in recent years, there is still a significant knowledge gap in accurately assessing how this type of misinformation impacts public perception and behavior. Our research aims to address this issue by developing a machine learning approach to automatically analyze social media conversations about the COVID-19 vaccine and identify how these conversations react to misinformation. We have created a annotated dataset containing over 14,009 Twitter comments from forum discussions, and using this data in combination with a machine learning model, we have found that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art misinformation detection models when testing on generic forum discussion data. However, we have found that our model's performance is limited when applied to real-world scenarios, such as fact-check articles and news articles containing misinformation and its subsequent corrections. As such, our model is best suited for use in forum discussions and may require further development in order to be effectively applied in other contexts.

Advancements in attosecond science have been facilitated by the development of few-fs high-harmonic generation, yet it is hindered by the formation of multipulse trains. Research into attosecond time-resolved strong-field phenomena requires isolated bursts of higher-harmonic radiation. A strategy has been developed to control the emission of isolated attosecond pulses using strong-field few-fs pump pulses, achieving a record 14-as pulse via temporal strong-field modulation.

Eclipse predictions for binary star systems are essential in identifying potential companions. However, secondary eclipses are often missed or misinterpreted due to the presence of multiple sources, particularly when one source obscures another. As a result, mass ratio constraints can be impossible to determine, limiting the accuracy of eclipse forecasting. This research addresses this issue by introducing a novel method that takes into account the nuanced characteristics of binary systems to predict eclipses for complex systems, including those composed of unequal eclipsing binaries. This approach can also detect potential new companion candidates by analyzing residual light variations. When applied to elusive quadruply eclipsing system AL Cet, the method predicted previously unseen eclipses with a high degree of accuracy, matching observed data. Notably, the method successfully identified a potential new low-mass object with a minimum mass of 0.14 MJ.

This paper investigates blow-up solutions to the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a mass超临界 nonlinearity and a spherical convex obstacle. By utilizing the variational approach, we develop the method of Pohozaev type to transform the problem into an infinite-dimensional minimization issue, focusing on the energy of stationary solutions. Furthermore, using the theory of Lagrange multipliers, we transform the problem into an unbounded optimization problem, allowing us to apply topological arguments, such as Lax-Milgram's Theorem and a version of the Morse theorem, to show the existence of solutions under specific assumptions. Our approach diverges from a method originally proposed by S. Cuccagna in his 2003 article "A variational approach to the Schrödinger equation with a spherical obstacle."

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements in convergence rates and computational efficiency are necessary to unlock its full potential. To address this need, our adaptive node generation method, RANG, utilizes residual analysis to pinpoint areas where the current approximation falls short in accuracy. As a result, RANG enables PANNs to concentrate their learning efforts on these critical regions. Efficacy of RANG has been validated across three complex three-dimensional flow problems, demonstrating its ability to significantly improve computational efficiency and accuracy.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of Multi-Domain ferroelectric FETs (FeFETs) in the sub-threshold region. Initially, the concept of Negative Capacitance (NC) in a monodomain FeFET is explained, in which the inversion layer is formed by the entire thickness of the ferroelectric (FE) layer. Subsequently, the principles of NC in multi-domain FeFETs are outlined, where the domain wall acts as a conductive path facilitating a local electrostatic response in the channel near the gate oxide. The local electrostatics are modeled using a phase-field approach, which is validated by comparing the simulations with experimental data on Negative Capacitance transistors and demonstrating the sensitivity of the model to various input parameters. Moreover, the possibility of hysteresis in the sub-threshold region is discovered. By leveraging molecular dynamics, the pinning of domain walls is modeled, giving rise to the characteristic V-shaped Transfer Transfer Characteristics (TCs) of FeFETs.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerabilities spread within it. Existing studies on third-party library vulnerability propagation have primarily focused on specific programming languages, leaving a crucial aspect of Cargo, a prominent package manager for Java, untouched. To bridge this knowledge gap, we propose a method to construct a Cargo vulnerability propagation knowledge graph and propose metrics to analyze vulnerability propagation patterns. By applying these metrics to the Cargo ecosystem, we uncover novel findings, emphasizing the economic implications of CVM and highlighting the emergence of CSEM as a more effective prevention strategy than SEM due to its potential to prevent secondary attacks. Furthermore, we discovered that vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies are often neglected in practice, and our analysis highlights the common reasons why CSEM has yet to gain as much attention as SEM.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subject to jump-type noise, our research establishes an essential ergodicity criterion based on irreducibility and Sierka's criterion. This result is applicable in scenarios involving pure jump noise and relates to stochastic systems experiencing complex dynamics.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the cosmic ray environment around 10^11 GeV. A detector prototype has been proposed that would measure key observables, including total cross-sections, charge symmetry, long-range Motteller range, pseudorapidity density, and p_T spectra.

Deep learning models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are widely used for image recognition, but their performance can be hindered by images with varied orientations. To address this limitation, researchers have explored learning rotation-invariant patterns, but this approach is computation-intensive, especially for remote sensing images. To overcome this issue, a novel model, the Orientation Convolutional Network (OCN), is proposed, which uses oriented filters in the first layer and standard convolutional layers in the rest, enabling the network to explicitly learn patterns with specific orientation dependencies. The OCN can also incorporate transfer learning, leveraging the abundance of normally-oriented images to improve its performance. Experimental results show that the OCN outperforms CNNs with rotation-invariant pooling, particularly with oriented images and when employing transfer learning.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We first reformulate GCN layers to gain mathematical clarity and subsequently derive a more efficient graph convolution. By doing so, the number of operations can be reduced to a linear function of the hidden units, facilitating the processing of large point cloud inputs. Our formulation also offers greater design flexibility for GCUs, as illustrated by the introduction of the Deep GCU unit. Moreover, our efficient graph CV approach is easily adaptable to existing GCU-based models, including DPGraph and GraphConv. Experimental results on various 3D object classification, segmentation, and semantic classification tasks, demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing GCU-based models, achieving improved accuracy and reduced computational complexity.

Recent advancements in the ubiquity of smartphones have enabled an extensive array of applications, which in turn has created numerous vulnerabilities for malicious activities. As a result, mobile applications have become prime targets for mobile trojan attacks, causing significant threats to mobile device users. While existing research on mobile trojan attacks is meaningful, it is primarily constrained to syntactic transformations, leading to limited detection bypass. Consequently, identifying and detecting such trojans becomes an increasingly challenging task. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel type of host-free mobile trojan attack known as the semantic trojan, which alters the underlying meaning of the mobile application code to evade detection by machine learning-based detectors. Specifically, the proposed approach exploits the over-fitting phenomenon in detector models by replacing trojan components with functionally equivalent components, thereby changing the data distribution and rendering detection impossible. Moreover, the proposed semantic trogen can not only bypass detector models but also achieve a perfect generalization rate, even on data that was not used during training. Empirical findings using real-world datasets validate the efficacy of the proposed semantic trogen, which presents a significant challenge for mobile trojan detection.

We are developing a new integral field unit for the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope. The integral field unit utilizes a custom-designed CCD-based detector with 256x256 optical fibers, each capturing a distinct point source, and a bespoke camera head to gather light within each fiber. This setup enables the simultaneous acquisition of up to 32 spectral bands within each point source, providing an enhanced 4D spectral dataset. Light within each fiber is split into two overlapping spectra by a grating, resulting in a combined dataset where one spectrum targets reduced wavelengths of 4600-7600 Angstroms with high precision, and the other targets reduced wavelengths of 4500-7800 Angstroms with enhanced resolution. The project involves innovative designs for the camera head and optical unit, incorporating both reflective and refrative elements, to achieve superior image quality within the compact space constraints of the IMACS spectrograph's camera. The integration of a custom-designed software package is also a key component of our integral field unit's development.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 55}, 390 (2019)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations through applying the Trojan horse method.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets similar to Earth. New studies focusing on the internal makeup of these planets rely on precise measurements of their masses. Precise stellar composition analysis is essential for precise mass measurements using the Seismic Mass-Gravity Relation. This paper shined light on the effect of stellar metallicity on seismic parameters, emphasizing the significance of accurate stellar composition. The research delved into how different elements affect stellar opacity, which in turn affects the star's internal p-mode oscillations. The study used SOHO and SDO solar data and found a relationship between metallicities and seismic shifts. The research also calculated mass and radius errors for planets based on stellar composition errors. For a star with solar properties, a 1% error in metallicity leads to a 0.08% error in mass and radius, while iron and magnesium have opposite effects. The research stresses the need for precise stellar composition, especially for small, low-gravity stars.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that only specific CSI metrics are capable of extracting relevant features for channel-based localization, indicating that using all CSI spectrum may introduce noise and hinder performance. In this paper, we suggest attention-assisted DNNs, which focus on CSI elements most indicative of distinct spatial characteristics. This approach enables the network to emphasize location-specific features and discard irrelevant noise. We also introduce a transfer learning-enhanced DNN to accelerate training, reduce training time, and prevent overfitting caused by large datasets. As a result, the performance of the attention-assisted DNN significantly surpasses that of conventional DNNs in various indoor scenarios.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.
