We investigate functions defined on the Hamming graph H(n,q) and subject to the constraints of the KQ polynomial constraint system. Our focus is on determining the minimum possible support size of such functions, and more specifically, on the function f of its support. It is proven that if the support of f, denoted as A, has a size less than the minimum possible support size, then the function values within A must be unique. Additionally, a few corollaries are demonstrated. The first concerns the non-existence of codewords with Hamming weight less than (q-1)(q-2)/6 in the Hamming metric within any [n,d,q]-code. Furthermore, it is proven that if d > n((q-1)!/((⌊d/2⌋!))²)/((d+1)!) then the code has the minimum possible support, i.e., every non-zero codeword has the minimum possible support. Lastly, a model of a tournament with a given score sequence and minimum possible support of size A is shown to have a score sequence that satisfies the Erdos-Gallai theorem, and also has a score sequence of at most |A| - 1.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users must install the software on their local machines. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing model loading and exploration without prior local installation. Web model loading is facilitated by importing from various sources, including local files, API, database, and repository mappings. Interactive model loading and loading status updates are key features of the service. Once loaded, users can run simulations, view results, and access COPASI's full exploration capabilities.

Deep Neural Networks have become an integral part of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to solve Partial Differential Equations and demonstrate reliable performance in various engineering and scientific contexts. However, the uncertainty quantification aspect of PINNs remains poorly understood, limiting the ability to generate confidence intervals for solutions, especially when dealing with complex problems involving data noise or parameter optimization uncertainties. This study aims to clarify the uncertainty quantification methods incorporated in popular Deep Uncertainty Estimation libraries, evaluating their performance in solving different types of problems and offering valuable insights to guide practitioners in selecting appropriate methods for solving Unclosed-form equations.

We are investigating operators within von Neumann algebras that correspond to class functions in the algebras of compact quantum groups. Our research specifically focuses on the class function von Neumann subalgebra within the type II factor constructed by Popa and Vaes from the property (T) compact quantum group $\mathrm{SL}_p(\mathbb{R})/ \mathrm{SL}_{p}(\mathbb{Z})$.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a reliance on precise linear system solutions and the calculation of the state transition matrix's high powers for value function computation. In our recent policy evaluation acceleration scheme, Inexact GMRES Policy Iteration (iGMPI), Inexact GMRES is utilized to approximate solution of the linear system, with the number of GMRES iterations typically scaling polynomially with problem size. However, the impact of inexactness on policy optimality can lead to an unbounded increase in iterations as the problem size expands. This paper explores the feasibility of a new algorithm, Informed Inexact GMPI, where a heuristic is applied to predict the value function's behavior, thereby enabling a controlled number of GMRES iterations, with the aim of balancing computational cost and policy optimality.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equal behavior.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of real-world processes. Specifically, it looks at cases where data are obtained from a computer simulator that generates time-series output, whose characteristics change based on a set of unknown input variables. Our goal is to determine the most likely values of these variables. Since directly calculating their distribution is impractical, we employ advanced estimation methods to approximate it. These methods involve estimating multiple dimensions of the distribution using multiple contour levels, which we propose utilizing a novel technique based on saddlepoint approximation. Through simulation experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in recovering the input variable distribution, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios, which are challenging for traditional methods.

Research has shown that certain distributional shifts can be devastating to machine learning models, particularly when they alter the relationship between input features and outputs. To tackle this issue, some studies have proposed using local queries, which involve making slight modifications to an instance and observing the resulting label changes, to gain valuable insights. Here, we investigate under what conditions local queries are beneficial for learning in the context of covariate shift. Our research demonstrates that local queries can enable learning from a single class of examples, even when they differ from those available in practice, by leveraging a grouping of queries. Moreover, we have derived a parameter that quantifies how local queries can aid in machine learning and discovered that this parameter is essential for both query-conditional and queryless learning scenarios. Additionally, we have found that when this parameter is small, query-based learning methods can be simplified and effectively executed using only a small number of local queries, as well as in absence of local queries.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically, events with a high-energy photon and a jet that passed through the nucleus, at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV per nucleon-pair. By comparing the results with proton-proton collisions, a notable change was discovered in the distribution of the energy of hadrons relative to the jet's direction. Hadrons with lower energies were more abundant than expected, while those with higher energies were less frequent. This observation supports the hypothesis that jets are altered as they pass through the quark-gluon plasma, with the degree of change increasing based on the angle of the jet and the density of the medium.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

A peculiar brown dwarf, known as WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 (hereafter J1534-1043 or "The Accident"), exhibits a confusing mix of features. Initially, multiple groups proposed a range of temperatures for this brown dwarf, from 600K to 800K, based on various photometric data. However, the results of the NEID long-term ephemeris study and high-resolution spectroscopy from Keck/HIRES have yielded a consistent age of approximately 7.7 billion years. This age, in conjunction with the PARSEC 3.19 model, suggests a mass of 0.077 M and a radius of 0.84 R for this brown dwarf. These updated parameters have enabled the re-evaluation of the bolometric luminosity and the incorporation of the Spitzer photometry into the SED, leading to a bulleted synthetic spectrum that closely matches the observed spectrum. This remarkable match implies a temperature of 565.5 ± 15K for J1534-1043, which was previously unaccepted. This novel temperature is a remarkable example of how synthetic spectra can effectively represent stellar spectra, particularly in cases where a broad band of continuum is present.

A study involving the L3b detector at the CERN LHC has yielded an initial measurement for the production of various particles including pions, kaons, proton, anti-proton and $\phi$ meson, in mid-peripheral Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV per nucleon-pair. Rapid distribution analysis shows that particle production is largely controlled by geometric factors, but deviations from this behavior are observed in the forward regions for higher-mass particles. The transverse momentum spectrum calculation indicates that these particles follow power-law patterns with a systematic shift towards lower momentum values compared to proton-proton collisions. The calculated ratios of particles to protons, specifically p/K+, p/K-, K+/K-, and $\phi$/proton, each exhibit distinct trends with respect to transverse momentum and also differ when compared to proton-proton collisions.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Selecting an in-situ construction method for Mars and the Moon presents a significant challenge due to difficulties in processing local regolith with existing equipment in an in-orbit environment. A potential in-situ manufacturing method involves using binders to create parts directly through mold-based composite manufacturing. In this approach, the filler material functions as the skeleton of the part, making the choice of local regolith as a sustainable and adjustable factor to modify mechanical properties and microstructure pivotal to improving final part quality. This study investigates how the sintering temperature affects mold-based composites made of thiol-based polymers and mixed with Martian and Lunar regolith in specific ratios. By placing the molds in an oven, researchers found that the binder-cured parts exhibited an in-situ sintering process that affected their mechanical properties. X-ray computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy were used to analyze and compare the binder and filler interactions, as well as the effect of sintering temperature on the composite's microstructure. The experiment showed that both types of regolith function effectively as fillers in the molding process and that the mechanical properties of the composite parts increased with higher sintering temperatures up to 723 K, beyond which the parts began to crack.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber are investigated, focusing on how slip at the liquid-solid interface affects the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in both the slender-fiber and thick-drop limits. This is particularly relevant when the film thins due to evaporation or other processes. By utilizing the exact solution of the axial pressure profile for the slender-fiber limit, we confirm that slip enhances flow rate and breakup time compared to no-slip conditions, especially in the very slender-fiber limit. This slip-enhanced behavior persists and is analyzed in the thick-drop limit using a drainage equation. Furthermore, we investigate the interplay between Rayleigh-Plateau instability and film thinning by representing the evolution of a dimensionless breakup number. This dimensionless number captures how Rayleigh--Plateau times vary with a liquid column length and how it depends on slip and Bond numbers.

By combining observations from the VLT and KICSS-2, we've identified a sample of nearby star-forming galaxies and measured their Balmer emission lines. This process involved a two-step procedure, initially using SED fitting to derive synthetic Balmer emissivities and subsequently comparing those with measured values in the Brackett-$\gamma$ continuum. Our analysis revealed that the B$\gamma$/H$\alpha$ ratio effectively separates star-forming galaxies from AGN, validating B$\gamma$/H$\alpha$ as a reliable diagnostic tool for recent star formation rates in the 3-5 $\mu$m wavelength range.

This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a vast number of type II subfactors with quantum dimension. The dimension of each type II subgroup is associated with the quantum dimension of the fundamental representation of sl_N at a root of unity. To achieve this goal, the authors develop a method to describe symmetries of local sl_N modules, offering an improvement upon existing methodologies by Gaudin, Molev, and Zhabitin. This innovative approach not only simplifies the description but also enables the identification of local sl_N quantum subgroups for all N, thus surpassing the previous constraints.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher in 1937 to model the spread of a gene, but also applies to various scenarios such as species competition, population growth, and disease spread. Despite extensive research on the Fisher-KPP equation, a significant gap remains in finding analytical solutions, which are crucial for understanding model dynamics. We utilize the conformal symmetry approach to reduce the Fisher-KPP equation and discover two new subspaces. Through solution methods like traveling wave transformations, we obtain novel exact solutions. Combining these with existing results, a comprehensive set of solutions is identified. We categorize the obtained solutions and visualize them graphically, demonstrating that closed-form exact solutions are feasible for Fisher-KPP equations.

In recent years, there's been an increasing interest in using smart devices to analyze handwriting due to its potential applications, like identifying handwritten mathematical terms. These terms are typically captured from a device, like a tablet, that has sensors, which record dynamic information about how they're written. This study proposes a new approach for classifying mathematical terms by analyzing the sensor data they produce, using a combination of hand-crafted features and a machine learning model to accurately detect the written terms. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on a new dataset, known as HSMD, that contains sensor data for handwritten mathematical terms, along with related processing and feature extraction procedures that result in a high-level accuracy of 89.51%.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and duration features, this new approach models durations directly at the audio sample level, allowing for the use of raw audio data without the need for phonetic alignment. We explore the effects of using different training strategies, including feedback control, and demonstrate that the method works well with a minimal amount of data, offering new possibilities for speech synthesis.

Species distribution analysis relies heavily on occupancy models in ecological studies. To analyze these, a package called spOccupancy is available in R, which supports the estimation of complex spatial occupancy models through Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation. This package streamlines model specification and can be integrated into Bayesian computation tools such as Stan, Nimble, and JAGS. Additionally, it offers pre-defined options to estimate a range of models, including single-species, multi-species, and integrated approaches. To facilitate understanding, diagnostic aids like convergence monitoring, auto-correlation analysis, and trace plots are included in spOccupancy. The package is intended to run on up-to-date Windows versions and Mac OS, but may encounter issues with older Mac OS versions.

The Skincare project is an advanced interactive deep learning system designed to assist dermatologists in identifying skin cancers by analyzing dermoscopic images of moles. This innovative tool brings together expertise from the University of Oxford and University College London in Computer Science and The Royal Free Hospital in the UK. Using a vast dataset of over 120,000 images, the Skincare system has developed multiple deep learning models for detecting benign and malignant moles, as well as categorizing the type of malignancy. Our work outlines the technical challenges we overcame to integrate state-of-the-art computer vision technology into clinical practice, including advanced segmentation, model ensemble, inference acceleration, and sophisticated user-interface design. We present two possible user-interface formats: a 2D image display and a 3D visualization of the skin, which can help dermatologists verify and refine the system's diagnostic recommendations. We provide our final models, underlying data, and implementation code on the Skincare GitHub repository for your reference.

To capture the inherent uncertainty in a complex dataset, we apply Bayesian autoencoders, a method that incorporates intrinsic variability in neural networks using probabilistic elements. Focusing on Type Ia supernovae from the Joint Dark Energy Mission Analysis sample, we utilize Bayesian and conventional autoencoders to capture the most informative aspects of the data, capturing intrinsic variability in the SN Ia population. By analyzing the recovered latent vectors, we identify the most significant factors contributing to variability in the data, discovering that a fourth dimension may be necessary to accurately represent the population. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the features extracted from the latent space can reduce scatter in distance modulus residuals by approximately 0.15 mag when used to train light curve fitters, indicating an enhanced ability to constrain cosmological parameters in the future.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy, which was detected using VLT/MUSE. The outflow, which has a mass of approximately 6.3e8 Msun and expansion speed of 560 km/s, surrounds the galaxy and is confined within a radius of 1.2 kpc. The outflow is well-mixed with the galaxy's interstellar medium and its distribution appears to be pressure-supported. This outflow has a total mass outflow rate of approximately 2.7e3 Msun/yr. The outflow is present in a galaxy with high star formation rate and a highly top-heavy stellar mass function. This mass outflow may play a crucial role in the physical feedback mechanisms that regulate star formation in galaxy evolution.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink slower than the fluid moves, researchers used numerical simulations to investigate factors like particle size, density, and the number of particles. They developed a new method to calculate the fluid movement rate, which takes into account how heavy particles affect the plume's behavior. They discovered that when the difference between the movement of the fluid and the heavy particles is not too significant, the fluid movement rate increases compared to a plume without particles. However, when the difference between the movement of the fluid and the heavy particles is significant, the fluid movement rate decreases compared to a plume without particles. They created a method to predict how heavy particles affect the fluid movement rate, which works for various types of plumes and conditions.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within complex networks, such as hypergraphs, offers valuable insights into potential outcomes. In this research, we analyze extinction thresholds of epidemic models, including the SIR model, on a class of 3-uniform random hypergraphs. By leveraging a recent development that connects hypergraph spectral parameters to epidemic models, we establish the asymptotic extinction threshold. Additionally, we introduce a new micro-critical phase and contrast it with the well-documented branching process phasemore >>

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, notably the observation of in-plane ferromagnetic order, have enabled intricate investigation of their electronic properties. The ability to manipulate magnetic order through layer number and orientation offers a unique platform to explore dimensional reduction, chirality, and two-dimensional ferromagnetism. The established ferromagnetic order in CrI$_3$ allows for in-depth theoretical examination of a spin-orbit-ferromagnetic system, specifically the influence of Rashba-like terms on Rashba ferromagnetism and electronic transport. By applying state-of-the-art ab-initio calculations, researchers found that in a bi-layer CrI$_3$ with a chiral structure, the magnetic order induces non-zero out-of-plane spin components within the electron wavefunctions, giving rise to in-plane ferromagnetic spin-orbit coupling. The RKKY interaction between these Rashba ferromagnetic layers, derived from their spin texture, is also analyzed. The research paves the way for further exploration of multi-component ferromagnetic order and its application in spintronics, particularly in tuning RKKY interaction through external magnetic fields.

To understand how magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars might form, we utilized the Pencil Code to develop mean-field solar-type dynamos within horizontally periodic boxes. These simulations employed anti-solar differential rotation and various helical turbulence configurations, assuming either local or non-local quantities. By analyzing the resulting cycles in terms of induction vector correlations and flow properties, we found that small-scale turbulent flows play a key role in dynamo action, regardless of the eddy viscosity model used. However, these models have different impacts on the overall behavior of these flows and the magnetic cycle itself. Specifically, the local scale model led to weaker turbulent velocities, longer periods, and fewer reversals, whereas the non-local model had the opposite effect, making it difficult for magnetic cycles to form.

Deep multimodal learning has drawn significant interest due to its ability to process complex, high-dimensional data. It has shown promise in addressing tasks that are difficult due to information incompleteness, such as multi-class classification in deep learning. Notably, the K-fan model, an extension of one-vs-all deep learning, has been proposed to efficiently handle multi-class tasks on complete data by training K independent models, each mapping its respective class to a k-dimensional vector space. However, deep multimodal tasks often involve complex feature interactions that can aid model performance, yet the K-fan model does not leverage shared representations across input modalities. To bridge this gap, a new model called Gk-fan is presented, which incorporates a representation sharing unit within each class to project diverse modalities into a unified k-dimensional space, thereby facilitating the learning of optimal modalities for their respective classes. Extensive experiments have demonstrated the efficacy and efficiency of the Gk-fan model compared to its counterpart Gk-fan-S, highlighting its superior performance in terms accuracy, convergence speed, and overall robustness.

The use of model checking has become an essential tool for verifying the correctness of single-threaded applications, yet it remains underutilized in detecting bugs in multi-threaded code due to the complexity and scalability issues associated with exploring all possible execution paths. Existing solutions often struggle with the vast search space, leading to inefficiencies and limited utility. McMini, a novel model checker based on dynamic partial order reasoning, offers a breakthrough by providing a configurable framework for building efficient checkers for single- and multi-threaded programs. These adaptable checkers focus on targeted runtime scenarios, allowing for the efficient detection of bugs such as deadlocks, variable access inconsistencies, and self-interactions within individual threads. By allowing the definition and analysis of only relevant equivalences, McMini can be used to develop both traditional and novel partial order reasoning-based checkers, efficiently detecting a wide range of bugs while scaling well across a variety of programs. Our implementation, featuring a flexible protocol for defining equivalences, has been used to build several high-quality detecters, which successfully identified more than 700 previously undetected bugs in multi-threaded applications, outperforming state-of-the-art checkers.

The effectiveness of fact-checking in countering misinformation dissemination is being investigated, specifically in the context of a platform like WhatsApp that may limit the spread of misinformation through individual group constraints. This paper examines a scenario where false information spreads through random WhatsApp networks, and a centralized authority releases verified information within these networks, represented as either insiders or outsiders. The study utilizes stochastic processes and mathematical analysis to model and compare the durations of misinformation and truth dissemination.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. This corresponds to a class of branching processes called Mark-branching processes, which encompasses well-known models like the Yule process and a neutral variant of the Cisneros process. In these populations, we examine the frequency spectrum of alleles, specifically how its distribution is calculated. This is accomplished by adapting a previous method from branching process theory, leading to a system of integro-differential equations. By solving this system, we approximate the frequency spectrum distribution, which is then expressed as an infinite series. This approximation allows for the estimation of key parameters, such as θ1 and θ2, and is demonstrated using numerical simulations for various population models.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system outperforms the current best countermeasure systems on public benchmarks, specifically the Domain Adaptation Evaluation Platform (DAEP) and the Common Voice dataset.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a solution to cosmological problems through supergravity inflation. After estimating the number of possible locally supersymmetric effective field theories, this research evaluates their feasibility as inflationary models. The study assumes that moduli fields remain frozen during inflation and considers two scenarios: one where supergravity follows a linear expansion in extra fields, assuming large split between supersymmetric and gravitational mass scales, and one where non-linear interactions are significant and mass scales are comparable. The analysis reveals that most models undergo large non-perturbative events or fail to satisfy slow-roll conditions. However, some exceptions exist, particularly when non-linear interactions dominate and supergravity inherits from a 4D $\mathcal{N}=1$ Super Yang Mills theory, and when non-linear interactions are included with specific interactions involving exponential or polynomial non-supergravity kinetic terms.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as leading platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to implement near-term error correction using quantum codes, necessitating precise calibration and measurement tools. In this context, we employ terahertz photothermal microscopy to calibrate coplanar waveguide resonators with high spatial resolution, revealing critical parameters. This photothermal method harnesses laser light to detect thermal emissions from the sample, facilitating contact-free and contactless measurement in radio frequency and microwave frequencies. Our findings include photothermal microscopy' ability to map resonances, map Q factors, and measure local magnetic field amplitudes within superconducting circuits. This novel technique bridges the gap between radiometric and optical imaging, enabling resolution of microscale quantum devices in their operational frequency range.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb R$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that $\aleph_1$ sets work, and our research shows that the size of such a division is limited to $\aleph_2$ only under specific conditions of regularity. Theoretically, we have found a partition of $\mathbb R$ into $\aleph_3$ sets, and this result can be achieved through specific forcing extensions.

In the realm of financial markets, maintaining a competitive edge may not be a hopeless endeavor. A more nuanced viewpoint could be that markets operate as adaptive systems, influenced by the entry of diverse investors who develop and implement varying investment tactics. By employing agent-based models, researchers can explore how multiple investors interact and which strategies persist over time. Our investigation utilized three such models - an order-driven market, a double-auction market, and a limit order book - featuring three investor types: market makers, random traders, and direction-following traders. Our double-auction model revealed that direction-following investors actually do not exploit market information and actually incur losses when active, in contrast to existing literature. Conversely, our limit order book model showed that direction-following investors do exploit information and actually enhance other investors' profits.

Identifying the application protocol being used over a network is crucial for detecting anomalies and ensuring seamless communication and data transmission. The dynamic nature of modern applications and networks complicates this task, as new and evolving communication protocols make it challenging for automated systems to accurately identify protocols. This paper examines the vulnerabilities of two prominent open-source network monitoring tools when it comes to dynamic protocol identification. Our research reveals that these tools can be deceived into misidentifying open sessions and employing countermeasures to evade such attacks. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a novel approach based on graph machine learning that outperforms existing methods. Our findings reveal that this new approach surpasses the performance of two open-source network monitoring tools.

Electrostatic gating is a common technique for controlling spin waves in thin magnetic layers. However, another method called superconducting proximity effect gating has rarely been explored before. The spin wave attenuation in a ferromagnetic layer increases due to the superconducting effect when a thin superconductor is placed beside it, but it is efficiently eliminated at higher frequencies. By utilizing this frequency-dependent behavior, one can superconducting gate effectively eliminate losses and control the spin waves, an ability that has significant potential for applying magnons in microwave devices. Our proposed approach offers a versatile platform for the manipulation of magnons and paves the way for magneto-electro-thermo-static convergence.

As deep neural networks are continually being improved with new classes added, centralizing all data for training becomes computationally impractical. This issue is exacerbated within the context of federated learning, where multiple clients hold disparate data, each representing different novel classes. We focus on addressing this challenge in federated learning for audio classification by proposing a method for handling new classes. Our method equips each participating client with a reference, allowing them to effectively tag known classes. It also enables non-participating clients to identify new classes independently. The proposed framework is evaluated through applications on audio classification tasks involving mixed datasets.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are employed. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces. To tackle this complex channel estimation challenge, which involves a high number of channel parameters to estimate, we propose an efficient approach called sparse estimation. Initially, this is achieved by transforming the channel into a sparse domain and then applying a least-minimum-average-absolute-error criterion to derive a solution that minimizes the overall estimation error. To mitigate the high computational cost associated with this method, we introduce a novel algorithm called successive over-relaxation least-minimum-average-absolute-error. Our proposed method is showcased through numerical simulations, which compare it to an existing algorithm known as least-squares minimum-average, demonstrating its superior performance.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring service of U.S. local news, examining how coverage of COVID-19 varied across different regions and correlated with infection and mortality rates, as well as audience engagement, between March 2020 and January 2021. Unlike previous studies of national media, our research found that local news outlets initially tended to cover the pandemic out of proportion to actual health risks but subsequently adjusted their reporting in a more proportionate manner. There was also a notable association between audience size and both the overall impact of COVID-19 on a region and the overall volume of local news available, indicating that these factors could be influencing how local media covers the pandemic.

The fundamental ability to count is a hallmark of human cognition. To model the gradual acquisition of counting skills in neural networks, we developed an artificial task where the relationship between inputs and outputs follows a complex pattern that changes after only a few examples. Initially, the trained networks struggled to generalize beyond their training data, exhibiting severe overfitting. However, by incorporating recurrent units into the architecture, the networks learned to retain essential intermediate patterns and successfully mastered the task. This simple test case provides insight into how higher cognitive abilities emerge through neural development.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming operations, such as database queries or database insertions. However, Bloom filters approximate set membership using bitwise operations, making it difficult to compress them. A new type of probabilistic data structure, the xor filter, addresses this limitation by allowing for a more compact representation. By substituting bitwise OR with XOR in Bloom filters, and then applying suitable linear algebra techniques, the size of the filtered representation can be reduced. To compensate for the loss of reversibility, we use bitwise NOR to verify set membership, leading to an improved variant of the xor filter, the xnor filter, which is faster and simpler to implement than previous methods. Our proposed algorithm for constructing and decoding xor and xnor filters relies on Gaussian elimination, resulting in an average time complexity of O(n^2 / m) operations. Our results show that the xor filter and xnor filter outperform previous methods on a variety of workloads, including database queries, map lookups, and constant-time single-instruction set machine operations. These findings are significant because they demonstrate that the xor filter and xnor filter are faster and simpler to implement than previously thought, leading to improved efficiency in single-instruction set machine environments.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and semi-divisor classes on a fixed projective variety, along with specific examples to illustrate and further develop divisor class properties.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to current prices, rather than relying solely on past price indicators. To validate this strategy, a quantitative analysis was conducted using historical stock price data, showing that prices are influenced by both past and future values, thereby supporting the idea that market participants anticipate and act on price trends, ultimately driving market movements.

This paper presents a privacy-preserving federated learning approach that's robust against data manipulation and noise interference. To protect individual user confidentiality, we employ Secure Multi-Party Computation, specifically utilizing Paillier encryption, to calculate virtual gradients from local model parameters. To mitigate the impact of malicious inputs, a statistical resistance method called FLVoogd is employed, which remains effective even with significant deviations from the expected normal distribution, as demonstrated through extensive testing. Furthermore, a novel federated averaging technique, which incorporates encrypted data, is proposed to update the global model, reducing the communication overhead compared to existing solutions.

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NEURON AI Challenge 2021 for end-to-end autonomous driving, utilizing a combination of traditional control techniques and deep reinforcement learning, along with a novel approach that bridges the similarity gap between simulated and real data, a significant hurdle in developing autonomous driving systems. The core challenge lies in the vast array of real-world scenarios that must be simulated for training, a computationally demanding task. The proposed method leverages environmental and vehicle state information, along with off-policy reinforcement learning and a noise injection technique, to make past simulated experiences more relevant to current scenarios, thereby enhancing training efficiency. Additionally, a network is employed to generate random noise and perturbate past observations to align with the current situation. The effectiveness of this approach was verified through a substantial dataset consisting of 1.5M driving episodes. The challenge evaluation benchmark, consisting of 300 episodes, yielded an average mean absolute error of 0.44 m/s, surpassing the winning benchmarks established at Neurons AI Challenge 2021. The complete code can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/Cheng-Wei-LinNEA.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes a novel deepfake generation approach that not only surpasses current methods but also adapts to various subjects, styles, and camera perspectives, making it more robust and applicable in the real world.

Identifying sub-Neptune exoplanets that are abundant and a vital step in understanding atmospheric evolution, which involves evaluating various formation and accretion processes. Employing the atmospheric compositions of two temperate exoplanets, which are detected through transit spectroscopy, which uses light from stars, which contains elements such as carbon, which combines with water to form solid compounds like carbonate, which affects the atmospheric composition. The analysis evaluates the role of planet formation and subsequent evolution, which affects the internal composition and composition of the atmosphere. The analysis considers two models: one incorporating ice-rich planetesimals and another incorporating chondrite material. The analysis applies these models to two temperate exoplanets, which are detected through transit spectroscopy, which considers the internal structure and composition of the atmosphere. The analysis applies this framework to two temperate exoplanets, which are detected through transit spectroscopy, which takes into account the composition of the atmosphere. The analysis applies this framework to multiple atmospheric models, which considers the composition of the atmosphere. The analysis applies this framework to multiple atmospheric models, which takes into account the composition of the atmosphere.

Despite the exceptional representational capabilities of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), their ability to learn from sequential data, particularly in unsupervised settings, remains an open challenge. Inspired by the novel capacity of spiking neural networks to emulate unsupervised learning of temporal patterns through the endogenous dynamics of neurons and synaptic connections, this research aims to uncover the potential of simple spiking neural networks to learn and reproduce basic temporal dynamics. It is demonstrated that, in two-dimensional grids of coupled Hodgkin--Huxley model neurons, specific sequences of discrete symbols can be encoded, represented, and learned using a combination of reliable single-neuron spike trains and coherent multi-neuron synchronized activities. The resulting symbolic sequences are represented by consecutive sequences of time-of-first-spike (TOFS) vectors, which are automatically extracted from experimental data without any prior assumptions. The network's ability to generate specific, complex temporal patterns, such as those of a specific character typed on a keyboard, is also illustrated.

This paper reports the findings of a collaborative study involving the NLP communities, which aimed to assess the NLP system's resilience to unexpected vocabulary during real-world applications. Ten challenging news articles with unique and novel terminology were selected to define a rigorous baseline for the challenge. A total of 87 NLP systems from 43 developers participated in the challenge by submitting their models to a thorough evaluation on four demanding tasks using the complete vocabulary of the ChID benchmark. The evaluation results revealed that most participating NLP systems struggled to effectively handle the limited out-of vocabulary dataset, with no single model emerging as a clear leader. Notably, seven strategies for tackling novel vocabulary were identified and tested, revealing mixed success in improving performance. The challenge findings can be accessed at nlg-challenges.github.io/chid.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent tracking problems and examining the stability of solutions in various other tracking tasks.

The goal of the proposed adaptive algorithm is to identify and isolate anomalies in a complex system with unobservable interactions. Specifically, the algorithm aims to identify sudden changes in a set of high-dimensional changes, where the probability of any two simultaneous changes is negligible. Following each change, the algorithm estimates the current system state and detects the moment a new regime begins. This approach is applicable to complex systems with unknown interactions, characterized as a graph where the nodes represent partial observations. Due to such complexity, traditional sequential change detection methods are impractical, so the algorithm employs a more manageable approach by designing a generalized likelihood ratio detector that is executed in a sequence of disjoint time frames.

We've created a detailed analysis of the galaxy populations in the Coma cluster, focusing on their properties and interactions, using the DESI DESI simulation. The artificial galaxy population we created mimics the real observed features of the Coma cluster, allowing us to study the relationship between galaxy properties and the forces that shaped them. The artificial galaxy population is divided into two main groups, similar to the dwarf galaxy populations we see in the local universe, with distinct properties resulting from different interactions. By analyzing the properties of these groups, we gain valuable insights into the formation and evolution of galaxies, as well as the forces that shaped them. The artificial galaxy population provides a valuable tool for studying the galaxy evolution and the galaxy formation processes, allowing us to test various models and theories. The artificial galaxy population is a valuable resource for galaxy researchers, allowing us to test various assumptions and models without fine-tuning. The artificial galaxy population is consistent with the observed properties of the Coma cluster, making it a valuable tool for galaxy archaeology. By studying the artificial galaxy population, we can learn more about the galaxy evolution and the galaxy formation processes, as well as the forces that shaped them. The artificial galaxy population is a valuable tool for galaxy archaeology, allowing us to learn more about the galaxy evolution and the galaxy formation processes.

We create a category, $C_G$, which is a modification of the tensor category, $cG$, of continuous linear Topological $\Bbb F_q$ - algebras, for a given profinite group, G, for each integral scheme, X, that's finite and flat over Spec $\Bbb F_q$, we associate a complex of $\Bbb F_q$ - TWC-spectra, for any integral scheme, X, a map, $\omega_X$, is defined, for all maps, $f$, from X to Y, that respects structure, in particular, $cG, acts on the spectrum, LXC/G, for any integral scheme X, a topological stable equivalence is shown, for all integral schemes X, $\omega_X, is established, enabling the development of homotopy fiber spectrum version of equivariant topological stable homotopy category.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process documents is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset for training. To overcome this, researchers employ semi-supervised training techniques, which utilize human feedback to refine the model's performance. However, current methods require significant human input to annotate entire document images, which can be expensive and time-consuming. In this paper, a novel semi-supervised approach is proposed, where human feedback is used to train the model to segment documents into smaller sections. Then, instead of labeling entire sections, only sample extracts from each section are labeled by humans. The remaining parts are automatically handled by the model. The proposed method employs a multi-task model that performs document segmentation and extract classification concurrently, with shared image encoders and cross-encoder modules for segmentation tasks. The segmentations generated by the model are used to improve the extract labels through human confirmation. The proposed approach significantly reduces the data labeling costs while maintaining the model's performance in document extraction tasks.

To analyze the bonding configuration and its effects on the EuS/InAs heterostructure, we employed resonant in situ X-ray scattering and first-principles calculations. The experimental and theoretical results indicate that Eu and As atoms form bonds across the interface in a specific orientation, resulting in the formation of a Tm-like 5d state and an In-like s/d hybrid state at the Fermi level, with the interface's total magnetic moment of 2 mu_B per formula unit. The evidence also suggests that the exchange interaction at the interface exceeds that in EuS by 0.25 eV, which could provide valuable insights for the search for Bose-Einstein condensation of magnons in magnetic insulators.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have enabled groundbreaking applications in science and industry. However, their high computational cost limits their widespread adoption, particularly when deployed on resource-constrained devices. Existing methods for reducing the depth and width of CNNs often fail to preserve the original structure or have excessive overhead. To address this issue, ClickTrain offers a novel structure-preserving pruning approach that can significantly and accurately reduce the depth and width of CNNs in a single training process. ClickTrain's primary innovation is a new placeholder data type called Click, which allows the compiler to optimize the entire training pipeline for efficient depth/width pruning. As a result, ClickTrain can achieve a 2.1x to 5.3x faster training speed and a 1.6x to 3.7x lower memory usage compared to the best existing methods, all while preserving the original model's accuracy.

This research examines the properties of specific modal logics derived from noncommutative lattices by incorporating $\Box$ and $\Diamond$. A new semantics model is introduced, specifically tailored for substructural modal logics. By applying duality principles, we demonstrate that every modal logic derived from the full Lambek calculus has a Kripke model, if it adheres to a specific semantic condition. Furthermore, we establish a dual relationship between certain mathematical structures, specifically modal algebras and topological Kripke spaces, utilizing a topological model developed from Priestley spaces.

The collaboration between observers of gravitational waves, electromagnetic spectra, and neutron stars opens up new insights into the universe. As the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors improves, it's essential to efficiently process the increasing amount of data. A new approach using deep learning, specifically a Residual Network, is proposed for detecting and categorizing neutron star-black hole mergers. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by training the network on simulated signals and comparing its performance with traditional matched filtering. The results show that the deep learning network can achieve a similar detection rate for NS-BH binary signals, outmatching existing methods. The detection efficiency of the deep learning approach significantly outperforms existing methods under various noise conditions. Additionally, deep learning classification of binary signals shows comparable accuracy with existing methods. The deep learning approach shows promise in classifying binary black hole signals based on mass ratios.

A new discovery has been made in the field of exoplanets: a gas giant called TOI-5542 b has been found using the TESS satellite. Research by the exoplanet community reveals that TOI-5542 is a small, old star located approximately 111 parsecs away in the direction of the constellation Carina. Observations by exoplanet hunters indicate the presence of a warm Jupiter called TOI-5542 b, which has a mass ranging from 0.29 to 0.90 times the mass of Jupiter, and it takes about 11.4 days to complete its orbit around its star. Studies suggest the planet has a radius of around 1.11 to 1.19 times the radius of Jupiter, and its surface temperature is estimated to be between 430 and 570 Kelvin. The mass and radius data of TOI-5542 b imply a dense composition, which could be attributed to the planet's formation in a metal-poorer stellar environment than expected, or its subsequent evolution involving the loss of outer layers.

Sequential decision-making in situations with multiple constraints can significantly complicate problems across various domains. To address this challenge, constrained Markov decision processes have been developed. By incorporating a penalty function into an unconstrained MDP, CMDPs transform into a constrained optimization issue, making policy iteration, dynamic programming, and gradient methods unsuitable for resolution. This paper introduces a new approach, the constrained Markov decision process augmented Lagrangian method, and demonstrates its theoretical foundations. Through alternating primal-dual hybrid gradient updates, the algorithm drives both the primal and dual variables towards optimal solutions. Given that CMDPs involve an infinite number of variables, the approach operates at the level of the value function. Moreover, a variant of the algorithm is developed for on-policy learning, and it is shown to enjoy global convergence under certain ergodicity assumptions. Simultaneously, the algorithm excels in data efficiency, and experimental results validate its superiority in various standard benchmarks.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when the dataset is limited, by combining several single-class neural networks and applying augmentation techniques. The approach uses a U-net architecture with varying image scaling and transformations. The influence of different activation functions on the neural network output was also examined. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated with a dataset of 108 mathematical symbols and compared to other neural network approaches. The results show that utilizing augmented data can improve recognition accuracy.

A geometric interpretation of superconformal quantum mechanics is developed, with the Hilbert space being defined by specific Dolbeault cohomology groups of a complex manifold, whose sizes increase in relation to the anti-plurissemicontinuous function's growth rate.

This research explores the impact of network complexity on the variability of a disease spread simulation based on the contact process. By examining the fluctuation dynamics of an SIS model in artificial networks with varied structures, the study investigates how network variability affects the behavior of disease spread. Artificial networks constructed with regular, random, small-world, and scale-free topologies were used to simulate the fluctuation of susceptible individuals. The results indicate increased variability in susceptibility as network complexity increases, contrasting with the predictions of mean-field theory, which assumed homogeneous mixing. Specifically, the variance in susceptibility deviates from the standard SIS model outcomes, demonstrating the significant effect of network architecture on disease spread variability.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is a popular off-policy RL technique, yet its standard implementation, utilizing policy gradients in the critic network, often struggles with exploration issues and unstable learning. To tackle these limitations, some researchers have turned to using off-policy correction methods like importance weighting, counterfactual value functions, and KL regularization in their exploration strategies, but these solutions come with high computational costs. To overcome these problems, this study proposes applying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMM) to the actor-critic RL framework, leveraging phase-space dynamics to facilitate more stable policy exploration and learning, without necessitating additional computations. Our method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art solutions such as KL regularization, counterfactual value functions, and importance weighting, showcasing its effectiveness through simulations in simple and complex continuous control tasks.

We will refer to the number $k$ that generates a given prime $p$ as its $\textit{generator}$. When two primes with a gap of $2$ are present, such as $6s-1$ and $6s+1$, their generator $s$ is ever-present. Our work is centered around the idea that a prime follows every pair of twin primes, i.e., if a pair of twin primes with generator $r$ exists, an prime with generator $s > r$ will also exist. This central argument underpins our approach to proving the Twin Prime Conjecture.

Twin primes with generator $0$ are clearly present, as primes like $3$, $5$, and $7$ demonstrate this, and numerous examples are found when $k \geq 6$. Autonomous navigation on complex terrestrial environments such as forests
relies heavily on precise real-time positioning data, which conventional methods
like SLAM often fail to provide at such times, especially when the robot
encounters challenging terrain. In an attempt to overcome this limitation, a
new approach is proposed that utilizes sonar data to enhance the global
positioning estimate derived from a Bayesian method while also providing a
real-time solution for the robot's orientation. Furthermore, integrating this
approach into a layered navigation system, utilizing multiple decision-making
algorithms, enables efficient navigation in difficult terrains, allowing a robot
to successfully traverse a forest environment and reach a designated
destination.

Nereid, a retrograde satellite of Neptune, possesses a highly eccentric orbit that takes it through varying distances from its parent planet. Its orbital characteristics enable Nereid to experience distinct thermal histories dependent on its orbital segments. Recent observations by the Submillimeter Wave Astronomy Satellite in far-infrared wavelengths place constraints on the composition of Nereid's surface, comprising water ice and other volatile compounds. Given the limitations of these observations, we assessed the water ice mixtures on Nereid's surface that best match its measured albedo using measurements from its Orbiting Near-infrared Spectrograph, observing that water ice and tholin are dominant components, with possible minor constituents such as CO2 ice or CO ice.

Lower triangular matrix rings of degree $n \geq 2$ over a commutative ring with a unity, denoted as $S_n(R)$, give rise to an affine space $\mathbb{A}^{|N||S_n(R)|}$, a projective space $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{A}^{|N||S_n(R)| +1})$, and consequently, an affine plane $\Pi_2(\mathbb{A}^{|N||S_n(R)|})$ and a projective plane $\Pi_3(\mathbb{A}^{|N||S_n(R)|})$. Our research reveals that these planes fail to comply with Desargues' theorem when the ring $R$ is not a field.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain real numbers can be constructed from a model of set theory to its extension, satisfying specific dominance relationships. Our research further expands on these findings by examining the nature of these real numbers within a framework of Tukey-order with models, a method introduced by Van Douwen and Huisinga. We prove that the sets containing minimal maximal Cohen and random reals, respectively, reach the highest level within this order structure.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline Bayesian methods rely on pessimism to ensure that their value function estimates do not exceed the optimal value function. This property is essential for guaranteeing that policy value does not exceed optimal policy value. This paper takes a different approach to pessimism, focusing on its minimization to identify the least restrictive policy value function that does not exceed the optimal value function. This paper presents a Bayesian method for pessimism optimization and investigates its consistency. Analytical and numerical results show that our approach leads to better average policy values than those achieved by the standard pessimism minimization method.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules, they result in established dualities between certain maximal subcategories. Consequently, this general theory unifies and extends previously defined dualities, such as the Nakayama duality and its generalizations, as well as dualities related to Gorenstein homological dimensions.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the Witting configuration's attributes.

To understand how superconductivity develops in conductive materials, researchers often study theoretical models with flat bands, but this is complicated by the involvement of complex interactions between particles. The aim of this study is to investigate many-body effects within a simplified two-dimensional flat band, resulting from a specific arrangement of hexagonal lattices without twists. The findings show that particle interactions within this flat band favor unique states: either conventional s-wave or unconventional d-wave superconductivity, depending on the type of particles involved. Contraction in the flat band leads to both types of superconductivity, with the d-wave type exhibiting characteristics similar to that found in cuprate superconductors.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and its square plus a constant times the quadratic character of an integer, denoted as $X+c\chi(-n)$, for all integers $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, where $X$ has a symmetric distribution on $\mathbb{R}$ and $c>0$. We prove this statement in the context of a locally compact abelian group, where elements have realvalued characters.

Presence-absence data is commonly collected in various survey formats, typically resulting in sparse binary matrices. Due to their high dimensionality, clustering these datasets can be problematic, particularly as they often contain numerous zero values. To address this challenge, we conduct a comparative analysis of different clustering methods, including those pre-processing techniques designed to handle the high dimensionality and zero-inflation characteristic of such data. By generating both pseudo-data sets in silico and analyzing a genuine dataset, we assess the accuracy of each method, thereby shedding light on the suitable approach for dimensionality reduction and clustering these particular types of data.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures, which can be inefficient. Our proposed method proposes an efficient framework that leverages pre-trained networks for both RGB and RGB-D setups, enabling efficient design. Our approach involves the integration of existing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and utilizes auxiliary tasks to generate a unified structure for salient object detection. Our method effectively combines color, texture, and depth cues to produce a salient map, which is further refined through post-processing. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our unified framework exhibits improved performance, exhibiting superior results on three standard evaluation platforms.

We are delighted to present our solution to the Identifying Offensiveness in Social Media (IDTOS) task at SemEval-2019. The experiment aimed to identify harmful tweets, their content, and the users behind them. A combination of BERT, SVMs, and feature engineering enabled us to achieve a F1-score of 0.7909 on the test dataset, surpassing the SemEval-2019 task's expected maximum F1-score (CEM) of 0.6662.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary representation, denoted as $N_k...N_1N_0$, meets the criterion where $N_i$ equals $N_{k-i}$ for all $N_i$. This paper delves into the effect of division by a palindrome, P, on both the binary expansion and numerical value of a number, N, where the quotient, Q, is an integer. Our analysis reveals that when a number, N, is divided by a palindrome, P, the quotient, Q, exhibits a binary expansion structure that can be expressed as $(q_{m-1}...q_1q_0)_{10}=(q_{r-1}...q_1q_0)_{k}*(q_{r-2}...q_1q_0)_{k}...*(q_1)_{k}*(q_0)_{1}$, where each quotient, $q_i$, is less than $q_{i+1}$ for all $i$. Our study examines various families of quotients, denoted as $Q_i$, and identifies cases, $i^*$, where the binary expansion $Q_{i^*}$ exhibits a palindrome, $Q_{i^*}=Q_{i^*}^R$, or an antipalindrome, $Q_{i^*}=Q_{i^*}^A$, characteristic.

Computed tomography (CT) uses X-ray projections from a rotating source to recreate cross-sectional images within an object's interior by exploiting their energy interactions. This process can be enhanced with a multi-detector array, which measures projections at various energy levels. Our study focuses on a non-convex reconstruction model that accounts for energy-dependent responses from both the X-ray source and the object. This approach allows us to reconstruct tomographic images using polyenergetic data sets obtained from multiple devices. The proposed variational model incorporates a total variation term to reduce noise from the raw data, material decomposition, which factorizes the exponential reconstruction equation into a linear system, and a source denoising term. The performance of our variational model is verified through simulated data, which demonstrates its capability to simultaneously reconstruct CT images, decompose materials, and remove noise from raw data, all while considering energy-dependent responses from the X-ray source.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) models are typically trained on limited datasets, which leads to overfitting. To mitigate this issue, state-of-the-art approaches utilize data augmentation techniques, specifically generative models. However, these solutions necessitate substantial amounts of labeled data to fine-tune the augmentation, posing significant challenges in scenarios involving low resource HTR tasks. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach based on the use of description graphs to generate training data. By leveraging graph-based descriptions to accurately represent the structural and compositional aspects of handwritten text, our method enables the generation of realistic samples without relying on any handwritten samples. We then employ a graph-to-image model to generate diverse training data. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct experiments on low resource HTR tasks with limited resource constraints, achieving improved results compared to other approaches. To further validate our approach, we also release an open-access, handcrafted graph dataset specifically designed for these tasks.

We have developed a novel storage strategy that significantly enhances the computational efficiency of two key components, multi-dimensional single and double reduced density matrices, within the ab initio no-core shell model. This innovation allows us to effectively deal with very light nuclei, all the way up to zinc with Z=30 protons, at a computational cost roughly in line with that of oxygen with Z=8 protons. The new approach makes it possible to achieve convergence of calculated nuclear properties with respect to the size of the ab initio no-core shell model basis without increasing the dimension of the density matrices, at a storage cost scaling in a comparable manner. The rates of computational growth with respect to the number of protons and neutrons are in a reasonable and manageable ratio, thereby facilitating comprehensive studies of the nuclear properties of elements up to zinc.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological properties for understanding complex systems.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude for supergravity on the background of anti-de Sitter space and a five-dimensional sphere by applying the truncated Witten diagram expansion method. This approach involved starting with the known two-loop amplitudes of type IIB string theory on the same background. Our results confirm previously found amplitudes and also reveal new contributions to the spectrum of string theory on this background, offering additional constraints for spectral analysis.

High-performance computing on high-end GPUs relies heavily on the ability to shift data between different memory spaces. For Python, this ability is limited as the built-in memory allocator on CPUs doesn't support moving data in parallel, which holds back the potential for accelerating application development. Despite this challenge, some research has explored integrating high-speed GPU memory into application development. However, this work has not focused on accelerating the underlying memory allocation process for C++ programs, a critical step in bringing GPU memory to application development. In response to this need, a new high-speed memory allocator named DynaSOAr has been designed specifically for object-oriented programming on GPUs. Unlike traditional memory allocators, DynaSOAr can run on GPUs and is optimized to copy pointers in parallel, which allows it to outperform the default GPU memory allocator by up to 2.02 times, 3.51 times, and 6.54 times in testing scenarios. Additionally, DynaSOAr is compatible with Python, allowing the use of Python's built-in features to manage memory, which results in up to a 2.51 times speedup and a 6.54 times improvement in objective function evaluation time.

We introduce and analyze a class of universal $U(1)_X$ extension models derived from $SO(10)$ GUT using various right-handed neutrino representations, with the aim of understanding the standard model's $U(1)_{Y}$ anomaly structure in terms of the new $U(1)_X$ symmetry. The models incorporate both fermionic and bosonic right-handed neutrino components, allowing for the exploration of their individual contributions to the gauge coupling evolution and neutrino properties. A key finding is that only a subset of models can naturally achieve a gauge coupling unification, while others introduce additional constraints on neutrino oscillation parameters through the absence of certain Higgs sector operators. The inclusion of right-handed neutrinos with spin-1 within an $SO(10)$ framework imposes stricter limitations on neutrino oscillation parameters due to the absence of specific Type-I seesaw terms.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields such as the social sciences, the prediction of 影响广泛的后果 is a challenging task due to the complex and uncertain nature of the system. The impact of an intervention on such systems can be severely affected by slight changes in the system's underlying assumptions. The issue is even more difficult when the decision-maker lacks access to the system's parameters and must instead draw from a set of possible credal networks. The variation in the system's response to the proposed intervention is a key concern, with the range of possible outcomes significantly affecting the confidence in the prediction. The slow growth of evaluation methods that can handle this uncertainty is a limitation, with current techniques being computationally expensive. The problem is addressed here by relating the uncertainty quantification to the verification of large-scale probabilistic circuits. The use of efficient constraint relaxation techniques allows the upper bound of the uncertainty to be determined within a specified time frame. The method offers two main advantages: reduced memory consumption and faster execution of the related queries. The uncertainty can be tightened over time with the help of a dual-based bound refinement technique. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through experiments on real-world datasets, showing significantly reduced memory usage and execution time. The method is particularly advantageous in scenarios where state-of-the-art evaluation methods are unable to complete the calculation within a reasonable time frame.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of vertices with distances measured by pair distances. If distances between any two vertices at a certain distance from a given point never exceed a certain quadiangle distance, the code is said to be neighbour-convex. A code distributes vertices evenly if every point has the same distance to the closest code element. A code that is both neighbour-convex and equidistributive is called neighbour-transitive. This work focuses on finding and classifying neighbour-transitive codes and partial spreads in generalised quadrangles of types X_n(q) through X_2(q). These codes satisfy constraints regarding their length, q value, and code size. A specific example of such a transversal code is a code whose elements don't share a common coordinate, specifically a Delsarte code.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX telescope, reveals significant anisotropy in gas density within this region. To quantify this anisotropy in two dimensions, a new correlation function has been developed and its application to the CMZ data shows that gas density is not uniform in its anisotropic properties. By comparing this anisotropy in density with that of velocity, it is evident that the morphological features of gas are not aligned in a single plane. Furthermore, this method has the potential to identify filamentary or ring-like structures at various spatial scales, providing a tool to map and quantify anisotropic features in interstellar molecular clouds.

Recent experiments involving high-harmonic X-ray production allow for new investigations into unoccupied valence electronic states in materials. To this end, we present a straightforward model for determining electron excitation rates in core electrons under intense, pulsed X-ray radiation, as utilized in experiments at the EXTREME Ultrahigh Harmonic Array source.
